title: Signed Integer Representation
summary: Sign-magnitude, one's complement, and two's complement all try to represent negative numbers in fixed-width bits — and only one of them let hardware reuse the same adder for both signs.

slides.markdown:
A register is a **fixed number of bits** — 8, 32, 64 — with no room for a `+`/`-` symbol the way you'd write it on paper. Every scheme for signed integers has to spend some of those bits encoding sign, and the encoding choice changes how expensive addition and comparison are in hardware.

The goal isn't just "can we represent negative numbers" — sign-magnitude and one's complement both can. The real question is **which encoding lets the same adder circuit work correctly for both positive and negative inputs**, so hardware doesn't need a separate subtractor.

slides.subTitle: Sign-magnitude
slides.markdown:
**Sign-magnitude** is the most literal translation of pen-and-paper notation: the top bit is a sign flag (0=positive, 1=negative), and the rest is the plain magnitude. In 4 bits, `0101` = +5 and `1101` = -5.

It's intuitive but breaks hardware in two ways: **two representations of zero** (`0000` and `1000`, both meaning 0), and addition needs an extra step to check signs and possibly subtract instead — you can't just feed both operands into a plain adder and get the right answer.

slides.subTitle: One's complement
slides.markdown:
**One's complement** negates a number by flipping every bit (bitwise NOT). In 4 bits, +5 is `0101`, so -5 is `1010`.

This fixes nothing about the zero problem — `0000` and `1111` both mean zero — and addition still needs a correction step: if a carry falls out of the top bit, you have to **add it back in** ("end-around carry") to get the right sum. It was a real improvement in symmetry over sign-magnitude, but hardware still couldn't treat signed addition exactly like unsigned addition.

slides.subTitle: Two's complement
slides.markdown:
**Two's complement** negates by flipping every bit **and adding 1**. +5 = `0101`; flip to `1010`, add 1 -> `1011` = -5.

This solves both problems at once: a **single representation of zero** (flipping and adding 1 to `0000` wraps back to `0000`), and — the big win — **plain binary addition just works** for signed numbers, no correction step. Add `0101` (+5) and `1011` (-5): you get `10000`; drop the overflow bit, leaving `0000` = 0. Correct, with the exact same adder used for unsigned numbers — why CPUs standardized on it.

slides.subTitle: Visualizing wraparound
slides.markdown:
Two's complement is easiest to picture as a clock face rather than a line: values wrap around instead of stopping.

![A 4-bit two's-complement value wheel, 0 through 15 bit patterns mapped to -8..7](assets/twos-complement-wheel.svg)

Going clockwise from `0000` (0), you count up to `0111` (7); one more step (`1000`) doesn't overflow to some undefined state — it lands on **-8**, the most negative value, and continues counting up (less negative) back around to `1111` (-1) and finally `0000` again. Overflow is just "stepping past the wheel's boundary."

assets.alt: A 4-bit two's-complement value wheel, 0 through 15 bit patterns mapped to -8..7

slides.subTitle: Why the range is asymmetric
slides.markdown:
An n-bit two's-complement range is `-2^(n-1)` to `2^(n-1)-1` — for 8 bits, **-128 to 127**, not -127 to 127.

The reason: there are exactly 256 bit patterns in 8 bits, and zero uses up one of them (only one representation, unlike sign-magnitude's two). That leaves 255 patterns split between positives and negatives — but the split isn't even, because the top bit pattern (`1000_0000`) is used for -128 with **no positive counterpart**, while every other negative value from -127 to -1 pairs with a positive from 1 to 127. One negative value is always "extra."

slides.subTitle: Negating in code
slides.markdown:
Negation is invert-and-add-1 — you can verify it by hand or in code:

```python
def twos_complement_negate(x, bits=8):
    return (~x + 1) & ((1 << bits) - 1)

twos_complement_negate(5, 8)   # 251 == 0b11111011 == -5 as signed 8-bit
twos_complement_negate(251, 8) # 5  -- negating twice returns the original
```

The `& mask` step truncates back to the register width, exactly as hardware would drop the overflow bit.

slides.subTitle: Comparing the three schemes
slides.markdown:
The deciding factor for hardware is arithmetic circuit cost, not representability:

| Scheme | Zeros | Needs a correction step to add? |
|---|---|---|
| Sign-magnitude | Two (`+0`,`-0`) | Yes — separate sign logic |
| One's complement | Two (`+0`,`-0`) | Yes — end-around carry |
| Two's complement | One | No — plain binary adder works |

Two's complement wins because it needs **one fewer circuit** (no dedicated subtractor, no carry-correction logic) while also removing the redundant zero — less silicon, fewer edge cases.

slides.subTitle: Negating INT_MIN
slides.markdown:
Because the range is asymmetric, **the most negative value has no positive counterpart in the same width**. For 8-bit `-128` (`1000_0000`): flip the bits -> `0111_1111`, add 1 -> `1000_0000` — you land right back on -128.

This isn't a bug in your math, it's the hardware faithfully wrapping around, and it's a real source of crashes: negating `INT_MIN` in C/C++ (`-INT_MIN`) is **undefined behavior**, and `abs(INT_MIN)` on a 32-bit int can silently return `INT_MIN` again instead of a positive number.
